content:
"Instead of disposing of garden prunings from your winter maintenance by burning or shredding them, consider transforming them into a dead hedge. This practical solution not only serves as an effective windbreak but also creates a safe haven for wildlife and helps delineate different sections of your garden. To construct it, drive stakes or old fence posts into the ground in two parallel rows, spaced about 50 centimeters apart. Then, layer the pruned material between them, starting with the thickest branches at the bottom. As you continue adding more clippings, the structure will gradually settle and become more compact over time.

Feeling disappointed with your Christmas gifts? Lift your spirits by reserving a copy of *The Book of Seeds* (Ivy Press, £30), authored by Paul Smith, the former director of Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank. Set to release in February, this visually stunning book offers an in-depth look at 600 of the planet’s most unusual and captivating seed species. Among them are the striking black seed with a hair-like appearance reminiscent of Donald Trump, as well as minuscule orchid seeds that are barely visible to the naked eye.

For those seeking winter beauty in their gardens, flowering clematis varieties can be a delightful addition. When planted in a sunny, sheltered location, these plants reward gardeners with vibrant blooms from December through February. *Clematis cirrhosa ‘Advent Bells’* (growing up to 3 meters tall and 1.5 meters wide) and *C. cirrhosa var. balearica* (reaching 2.5 meters by 1.5 meters) both produce creamy, fragrant flowers adorned with maroon speckles. Meanwhile, *C. cirrhosa ‘Jingle Bells’* stands out with its pure white blossoms and can grow as large as 5 meters by 2 meters, making it a striking focal point in any winter garden."
